body.html:
The booklet has three chapters for now: why study the history of medicine, the history of anatomy and the history of physiology. The same idea runs through all three: medical knowledge is produced inside a particular culture, with the methods available at the time, and what one generation takes for granted, the next may find mistaken.

The professor says it herself: the point is not to memorise a list of dates and names, but to understand how medicine became what it is. Still, the people, the turning points and the lessons drawn from them are what questions are built on.

title: Why study the history of medicine?
subject: subj:history

body.html:
The central paradox: the questions medicine asks (pain, fear, uncertainty, suffering, the wish to heal) have stayed the same, while the explanations and methods have changed profoundly. Medicine is shaped by science, but also by philosophy, religion, culture, politics, economics and how society is organised.

Three ways of explaining illness (they often coexisted rather than following one another):

  • Balance and harmony: health as equilibrium; in Greek medicine, the four humours.
  • Faith and divine will: illness as a test, punishment or spiritual event; religious institutions also gave care and shelter.
  • Evidence and technology: experiment, dissection, microscopy, laboratory tests and imaging.

Will future generations laugh at us? Past practices were sometimes based on wrong theories or kept by authority and tradition. Studying this should give intellectual humility, not a rejection of modern medicine: our knowledge stays open to revision.

Is medical progress always progress for patients? Four dimensions do not move at the same pace:

ProgressThe question
ScientificDo we understand the body and disease more accurately?
TherapeuticCan we prevent or treat illness more effectively?
EthicalAre patients treated with more respect and protection?
SocialDo the benefits reach the people who need them?

What history teaches future physicians: humility (knowledge is provisional), critical thinking (neither age nor novelty proves value), contextual understanding (illness is not only biological), ethical awareness (consent, dignity, protection from harm) and perspective (today's debates have historical roots).

title: Anatomy: from Egypt to the Middle Ages
subject: subj:history

body.html:
Anatomy comes from the Greek anatome, dissection. Interest in it has followed a wave-like curve, shaped by beliefs, science, practical needs and the chance to examine bodies. Structural changes do not always explain illness, and disease can occur without visible anatomical change.

PeriodKey points
Ancient EgyptSophisticated embalming gave practical knowledge of the organs, but for religious and funerary purposes, not systematic science. Practical knowledge does not necessarily lead to scientific understanding.
Ancient GreeceSculpture reached great precision in surface anatomy, but human dissection was generally forbidden or restricted, so knowledge came from external observation, clinical experience and animal dissection. Greek medicine stressed clinical observation and the four humours; Hippocratic treatises on fractures and dislocations show practical skill.
Roman period: GalenPhysician to gladiators; learned through observation and experiments, mainly on animals. Added to knowledge of muscles and nerves. Used teleological reasoning (structures exist for a purpose). His writings dominated teaching for centuries, but animal-based errors were repeated. Lesson: a source's reputation can outweigh the evidence.
Medieval EuropeChristian beliefs (the body linked to sin, bodily resurrection) limited dissection, though it did occur in teaching and examinations, sometimes on executed criminals. Galen stayed the main reference.

Renaissance: the 14th-century plague epidemics challenged old explanations of disease (but did not directly cause the revival of dissection). Dissection became more common and art and science converged: Andreas Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica (1543), revolutionised anatomical teaching; Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man explored the body's proportions. Later, sensualism (knowledge comes from the senses) encouraged collections of anatomical wax models, as in La Specola museum in Florence.

The paradox of early modern medicine: the body could be studied with great precision, yet this did not make treatment better. Practitioners often ignored anatomy, focused on symptoms, and lesions could usually only be found after death.

18th and 19th centuries: from art to clinical science

  • Percussion (Leopold Auenbrugger, 1761) and auscultation (popularised by René Laennec) let doctors detect lesions in the living body, e.g. linking breathlessness to a pleural effusion. Disease came to be understood in anatomical terms.
  • Anatomy became a medical discipline: university chairs, dissection central to training, though public opposition remained.
  • The body trade: legal bodies (executed criminals) were too few, so resurrectionists robbed graves (hence mortsafes). Burke and Hare murdered people in Edinburgh to sell bodies to the anatomist Robert Knox. This led to the British Anatomy Act of 1832, giving legal access to unclaimed bodies and regulating dissection. Japan legislated on body donation in 1983.
  • From stolen bodies to donation, seen as a social contribution; better preservation of bodies.
  • Gray's Anatomy (first published 1858, illustrations by Henry Vandyke Carter) standardised anatomical knowledge.
  • Late 19th century: women in some Irish medical schools had to dissect in separate rooms (modesty), which limited their access: education shaped by gender norms.

Today: medicine stresses function over structure; cadavers or digital simulation? Dissection also has a symbolic role, a rite of passage into the profession and respect for the dignity of the dead.

Lessons: knowledge depends on the methods available; authority must stay open to scrutiny; progress is cumulative but not automatic; anatomy is also the history of how humans learned to look at themselves.

Physiology (Greek physis, nature, and logos, study) is the study of the functions of living organisms: what is life, and how does it work? It breaks functions into smaller processes (digestion: intake, mastication, swallowing, digestion, absorption, metabolism, elimination).

DebateOne sideThe other side
The nature of lifeVitalism: a vital force that physics and chemistry cannot fully explain (sometimes linked to the soul)Mechanism: functions explained by physical and chemical processes
The purpose of lifeTeleology: explains structures by their purpose (why does it exist?)Empiricism: knowledge from observation and experience (how does it actually work?)
The methodSpeculation: reasoning and reflection without testingExperimentation: manipulating conditions, testing hypotheses, measuring outcomes

These were not mutually exclusive; physiologists mixed them in different proportions.

title: Physiology: Antiquity and the Middle Ages
subject: subj:history

body.html:
The four humours (Hippocratic tradition): health = balance, illness = imbalance in quantity, distribution or quality. Treatment restored balance by diet, exercise, bathing and, if judged necessary, purging or bloodletting. It lasted more than 2,000 years because it was a coherent system when experiment was limited.

HumourElementQuality
BloodAirWarmth
PhlegmWaterColdness
Yellow bileFireDryness
Black bileEarthColdness

Galen of Pergamon: anatomy plus a teleological view (every organ has a purpose). Three spirits (pneuma):

SpiritOrganFunctions
NaturalLiverNutrition, growth, vegetative functions
VitalHeartVitality, heat, maintaining life
AnimalBrainSensation, movement, higher nervous functions

Galen thought blood was made in the liver from food and consumed by the organs (no closed circuit), and passed from right to left heart through invisible pores in the interventricular septum.

Middle Ages: Galen's spirits fitted religious ideas of the soul, so his authority stayed strong. Ibn al-Nafis (13th century, Syrian physician) correctly described pulmonary circulation (right heart → lungs → left heart through the pulmonary vessels), but was little known in Europe. Michael Servetus (Spanish theologian and physician) described it in a theological work in 1553 and was burned for heresy in Geneva that year, mainly for his religious views.

WhoContribution
William Harvey (1578-1657), EnglishShowed that blood circulates continuously. Quantitative argument: the heart pumps far more blood than the liver could make; also ligature experiments on veins. The heart as a mechanical pump. Turning point: claims tested by experiment and calculation, not authority.
René Descartes (1596-1650), FrenchMechanism: the body as a machine (a sick man as an inaccurate clock). Mind-body dualism: res cogitans (thinking mind) and res extensa (material body). The soul acts on the body through the pineal gland. Animal spirits travel in nerves; he explained heart movement by heat and expansion of blood, unlike Harvey's pump.
Iatrochemistry; John Mayow (1641-1679), EnglishLife as chemistry. Candles and small animals in closed vessels: both depend on a limited part of air, anticipating oxygen. Lavoisier later established oxygen's role in combustion and respiration.
Luigi Galvani (1737-1798), ItalianElectrical stimulation contracts frog muscles: animal electricity, the start of bioelectricity.

Auguste Comte (1798-1857), positivism: knowledge from observable facts. Thought passes through three stages: theological (supernatural), metaphysical (abstract forces), positive (laws from observation). Physiology moved from asking ultimate causes to how and when processes occur.

  • Charles Bell and François Magendie: Bell-Magendie law (sensory roots carry information to the cord, motor roots carry commands to muscles). Magendie founded the Journal de physiologie expérimentale et pathologique in 1821.
  • Claude Bernard (1813-1878): founder of modern experimental physiology. Method: observe, hypothesise, identify the structure, test by experiment. Milieu intérieur (internal environment), the basis of later homeostasis.
  • William Beaumont (1785-1853), US army surgeon, studied digestion through the gastric fistula of Alexis St Martin (gunshot, 1822): digestion is chemical (gastric juice), not only mechanical.

20th century: physiology central to medicine. First Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1901, Emil von Behring (serum therapy against diphtheria).

Ethics: animal and human experiments, sometimes on prisoners, soldiers or vulnerable groups without consent. Nazi experiments led to the Nuremberg Code (1947): voluntary consent is essential. Declaration of Helsinki, first adopted 1964. PETA founded 1980. Progress is now judged also by how knowledge is obtained.

Neuroscience: Paul Broca (1861) linked loss of speech production to damage in the left frontal lobe; Wilder Penfield stimulated the cortex during surgery and drew cortical maps. How brain activity becomes conscious experience is still debated.

Lessons: knowledge evolves; methods transform knowledge; mechanism versus vitalism remains a key debate; progress raises ethical questions.

Epidemics shape economic, social, intellectual and political life. Society reacts in stages: denial and delayed acceptance → panic, terror, chaos and flight → explanatory frameworks and perceived causes → control measures → resumption of normal life with new knowledge and prevention policies.

Black Death: first large wave 1348, arriving from Asia by ship and killing about 30% of Europe; blamed on constellations, divine punishment of corrupt priests, travellers and minorities; perceived as contagious (flight from cities, mass graves). Bubonic plague: fever, swollen nodes, dehydration, death. Control: quarantine of ships and travellers, home confinement, plague doctors and pesthouses. Cause: Yersinia pestis, host the black rat, vector the flea — confirmed by DNA sequencing of old remains. Syphilis, the "French disease": outbreak in French armies in the 1490s, then Europe; painful skin lesions, recognised as sexually transmitted; love and death; scandalous early trials on prostitutes; Treponema pallidum, treated with penicillin, still not eradicated. Leprosy: the main example of induced social prejudice — excessive isolation (leprosaria, bells) for a mildly contagious disease; Mycobacterium leprae (Hansen's disease); still present; WHO global strategy 2016–2020 based on anti-discrimination.

Cholera: Europe and North America in the early 19th century; massive diarrhoea and rapid death; personified in the poor and immigrants, who were confined in unsanitary settings; the link with drinking water was established by John Snow in 1854; Vibrio cholerae identified 1884; still spreads where water is contaminated by sewage. Smallpox: endemic in Europe since antiquity, killed kings and peasants, used as a biological weapon (soiled blankets); controlled without knowing its cause thanks to two principles — it was inevitable and survivors were immune; Jenner's experiment (1798): cowpox (vaccinia) protects against smallpox (variola); the first human disease eradicated, 9 December 1979, with two remaining samples debated. Tuberculosis: main cause of adult death in the 19th century — wasting, fever, cough; sanatoria; McKeown (1970) questioned whether health workers deserved credit for the 20th-century mortality decline.

EpidemicAgentKey date / figure
PlagueYersinia pestis (rat, flea)1348, quarantine
SyphilisTreponema pallidum1490s, penicillin
LeprosyMycobacterium lepraeHansen; WHO 2016–2020
CholeraVibrio choleraeSnow 1854; 1884
SmallpoxVariola virusJenner 1798; eradicated 1979
TuberculosisM. tuberculosis19th c.; McKeown 1970
InfluenzaInfluenza virus1918, 25–100 M deaths
AIDSHIV1981, GRID

Influenza 1918, the "Spanish flu" that did not start in Spain: 25–100 million deaths; new institutions and policies for epidemic control. AIDS: emerged in the USA in 1981 among homosexual men, first called GRID; millions of deaths, especially in Africa; the "innocent vs guilty victims" idea; years of delay before credible investigation; questionable control (Cuba's sanatoria); antiretrovirals cut deaths but eradication is far off. COVID-19 invites comparison with the plague and reflection on what humanity has learnt. Other global epidemics: Ebola (1990s), bilharzia (1970s), mad cow disease (2001), swine flu (2009). The Moroccan oil tragedy (1959): an acute epidemic of four-limb paralysis affecting whole families, in Meknes then the Rif and elsewhere.

The human side of care begins with observation. Confusion: raised or drawn eyebrows with forehead creases, narrowed unfocused eyes, mouth partly open, head tilted. Fear/scare: wide eyes, raised or furrowed brows, tense mouth, pale face. Anger: narrowed eyes, furrowed brows, clenched jaw, pressed lips or bared teeth. Confidence: relaxed steady eyes, slightly raised brows, small closed-lip smile, chin lifted. Disappointment: downcast half-closed eyes, lowered brows, downturned slack lips, low energy. Sadness: pained brows, drooping lids, watery eyes, downturned mouth. Contempt: one raised eyebrow, sideways narrowed glance, curled lip or sneer, head tilted back — a mix of anger and disgust. Disgust: wrinkled nose bridge, lowered brows, curled upper lip, tongue slightly out. Surprise: wide eyes with dilated pupils, arched brows, open mouth. Patients' expressions can conceal as much as they reveal; empathy expands what the observer perceives — "observation is attention with intention; when we slow down to see, we begin to understand."

EmotionKey facial cues
ConfusionDrawn/raised brows, forehead creases, unfocused eyes, tilted head
FearWide eyes, raised/furrowed brows, tense mouth, pallor
AngerNarrowed eyes, furrowed brows, clenched jaw, pressed lips
ConfidenceRelaxed eyes, small closed smile, lifted chin
DisappointmentDowncast half-closed eyes, lowered brows, slack downturned lips
SadnessPained brows, drooping lids, watery eyes, downturned mouth
ContemptOne raised brow, sideways glance, curled lip, head tilted back
DisgustWrinkled nose bridge, curled upper lip, tongue slightly out
SurpriseWide eyes, dilated pupils, arched brows, open mouth

Five keys to emotional intelligence: self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, social skills (and motivation). Self-awareness covers your social style (pragmatic/performance-driven vs humanistic/relationship-driven), personality (e.g. accepting or declining group study, panicking or calmly structuring a last review), emotions (name the main emotion and the physical sign that reveals it — e.g. when asked about the median nerve in front of peers), values/motivation and mindset (toward personalities, stress, emotions and relationships).

Emotional self-regulation empowers thoughtful acting over reacting. Short-term tools: mindfulness, conscious breathing, postural change, cognitive break, cognitive assessment, sensory grounding, positive self-talk. Long-term tools: proactive thinking, emotional journaling, emotional hygiene, positive visual imagery, cognitive empathy, self-compassion. Rephrase negative self-talk: "I made an honest mistake; this is frustrating, but I can fix it"; "I need to refocus on priorities and ask for help"; "my ideas aren't always chosen — maybe I should get feedback"; "he may not want a friendly relationship with me, and that's OK."

Three dimensions: cognitive (perspective-taking: knowing what the other thinks or believes), emotional (standing in their shoes: feeling what they feel) and behavioural (compassion: willingness to act to help and relieve). Empathic replies name the feeling and offer presence: "I can see that really got to you; being corrected in front of everyone can feel embarrassing"; "it sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — let's break things down together"; "that sounds like a tough experience; if you want to talk it through, I'm here." Avoid dismissal ("stop overreacting", "just manage your time better") and false empathy that ends in "but you're wrong" or "you're off base".

DimensionNameMeaning
CognitivePerspective-takingKnow what the other thinks or believes
EmotionalStanding in their shoesFeel what the other feels
BehaviouralCompassionWillingness to act to help and relieve

Active listening; the art of disagreeing — it is fine to disagree, but with grace: do not try to convince the other you are right, try to understand how they feel, and treat their feelings as information to process; praising; conflict resolution with the Thomas-Kilmann model (balancing motivation to reach your interests against motivation to cooperate); and non-violent communication in four steps — observation ("when I was talking and you looked at your phone"), feeling ("I felt frustrated and unheard"), need ("because I need to feel listened to"), request ("would you be willing to put your phone aside for 10 minutes?").

Pathology (Greek: the study of suffering) is material knowledge about disease. It has always been practised, even unnamed, and in each era it was validated by the science and philosophy of the time. It has five universal functions: explain suffering (spiritual beliefs such as sin and blame, or scientific grounds — structure, function, heredity, contagion), identify the ailment (diagnosis: observation plus knowledge; defining the abnormal also defines the normal, and both concepts keep changing), predict outcomes (prognosis: once like divination, now statistical — mortality, survival, risk factors), justify treatment (rationales usually applied post hoc; the remedy persists while the explanation changes) and prove or refute an explanation (autopsies for retrospective diagnosis since the 13th century, widespread in medicine and law since the 19th — forensic pathology, malpractice suits).

title: Illness, disease, and theories of cause
subject: subj:history

body.html:
Illness is the patient's individual suffering — constant in time and space, patient-centred. Disease is the medical idea about illness — changing with knowledge, involving patient, observer and illness. Two families of cause-based theories: physiological (the inside — what the patient is) and ontological (the outside — what the patient has). Historical overview in four moves: supernatural causes, pathology at the bedside, pathology moves to the morgue, heredity strikes back.

IllnessDisease
What it isIndividual sufferingMedical idea (theory) about illness
Over timeConstant in time and spaceChanges with knowledge
WhoPatient-centredPatient, observer and illness

title: Supernatural causes and pathology at the bedside
subject: subj:history

body.html: Supernatural: ontological origins from higher powers to punish or test; the features of illness mattered less than the patient's idea of cause; treatment meant restoring integrity, righting wrongs, keeping faith. Religion still comforts patients, but also stigmatises (AIDS, addiction seen as deserved; chronic illness as a trial like Job's). Greco-Roman antiquity refuted the supernatural: disease as a natural imbalance of the four elements/humours; Hippocratic pathology worked with the best science of its time (explain, describe, predict, interpret, justify). The Sacred Disease (epilepsy) was declared no more divine than any other, with falling, shaking, loss of consciousness and incontinence attributed to phlegm obstructing the brain. Treatment restored balance: bleeding, diet, baths, fumigation. Galen's eclectic, vitalist pathology prevailed. Nosology: distinguishing diseases by symptoms — Rhazes separated fevers with and without rash (9th c.); the Renaissance saw the decline of Galenism and the rise of sensualism (iatrophysics, iatrochemistry) and uroscopy as a diagnostic tool; Sydenham described gout and dropsy; nosologists built classification tables where diseases became entities — more observation, less theorising.

Two centuries ago anatomy was irrelevant at the bedside: changes were hidden until death, might be caused by death rather than disease, and could not be repaired. In the 18th century autopsy served clinical medicine: Morgagni's The Seats and Causes of Diseases Investigated by Anatomy (1761), with an index of diseases and an index of organic lesions — anatomical pathology was born. In the 19th century symptoms were linked to anatomical changes (physical diagnosis); the disease concept shifted from the patient's feelings to the lesion found ("phthisis" became "tuberculosis"). From the 1830s the microscope classified disease by tissue change; Virchow described leukaemia (1846) and brought cell theory to pathology; diagnosis rested on findings — one could have a disease without feeling sick. Germ theory: Pasteur (link bacteria–disease), Lister (carbolic acid on open fractures), Koch (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Nobel 1905); the 1880s triumph of germ theory brought vaccines (Joseph Meister), a new concept of disease as external invaders, hospital laboratories and bacteriology as a discipline — yet infection also depended on the host, not only the invader.

title: Heredity strikes back and today's model
subject: subj:history

body.html: Heredity is an ancient idea overshadowed by germ theory; bacteriology → microscopes → cells → chromosomes → the discovery of DNA (Watson and Crick, 1952; Nobel 1962). Molecular pathology and nanomedicine, molecular types of cancer, new evidence of organic causes, and applications in paleopathology. The current model blends physiological (internal) and ontological (external) factors — epigenetics mixes both; extrapolation is dangerous, as it can blame patients or stigmatise communities, and the place of the subjective in disease remains a question. The case of phrenology (Franz Gall, early 19th c.) illustrates how a theory can be validated by its era and later refuted.

Pharmacology comes from the Greek pharmakon — drug, remedy, and poison at once — and is the science of drugs and treatments. Most therapies were found empirically: by observation, accident, and trial and error, with the constant problem of the placebo effect. Oliver Wendell Holmes quipped that sinking the whole materia medica to the bottom of the sea would be better for mankind and worse for the fishes. The first principle remains first, do no harm.

Early treatments belonged to mysticism and magic. Rationales changed with the understanding of disease: similia similibus curantur (like cures like — restoration of health, ancestor of homeopathy) and contraria contrariis curantur (opposite cures opposite — healing, but with side effects). Poison antidotes: Mithridate (1st century BC) and Theriac (therion = beast), which kept a mystical aura until the 19th century. Awareness of side effects grew: drugs vanished because of dangerous effects, and drug resistance appeared.

Greco-Roman treatment aimed to restore the balance of humours: non-drug remedies (diet, lifestyle, bloodletting, baths, exercise) and about 300 medications for internal or external use; Galen founded galenical pharmacology, trusting the healing power of nature. The advent of metals (15th century, influenced by alchemists): copper, sulphur, salt, mercury — mercury for syphilis, antimony for everything. Apothecaries were the ancient pharmacists, preparing and dispensing materia medica, mostly practised by women; botany remained a standard subject of medical education until the 20th century, with botanical gardens in hospitals and schools (Chelsea Physic Garden); most current drugs still derive from plants but are manufactured. Drugs were classified as poison vs antidote, by physical properties, or by physiological effect (laxatives, emetics, narcotics). The French Revolution pushed for pure drugs instead of complex mixtures, and the rise of surgery asked: why give a pill when you can cut and cure?

After germ theory was accepted, the search turned to vaccines and drugs against germs: antibiotics — Alexander Fleming's penicillin, in wide use by 1945. Hormones raised medical optimism through replacement of deficiencies: in 1922 Banting and Best, under Macleod at the University of Toronto and with Collip's purification, injected insulin into diabetic children in coma at Toronto General Hospital, who woke one by one; the patent was sold to the university for one dollar; Banting and Macleod won the Nobel Prize in 1923.

James Lind's scurvy trial (1747) was the prototype. Trials were formalised in the early 19th century with statistics; untreated controls (1900s); committees to ensure sound conclusions (1930s); randomisation (1940s); blinding and standardisation (after 1940); ethical protection with the Nuremberg Code (1947) — the road to evidence-based medicine. Recent scepticism: magic bullets brought magic problems — drug resistance, nosocomial infections, dangerous side effects; is the rise in life expectancy really due to drugs and anti-infectives? disillusionment with universal eradication. The thalidomide catastrophe harmed about 10,000 children in 25 countries; Frances Oldham Kelsey (1962) blocked its approval in the USA, showing that complex licensing procedures should not be blamed for slowing innovation.

PeriodAdvance in clinical trials
1747Lind's scurvy trial
Early 19th c.Formalisation with statistics
1900sUntreated controls
1930sCommittees for sound conclusions
1940sRandomisation
After 1940Blinding and standardisation
1947Nuremberg Code: ethical protection

Physiology (Greek: the study of nature) is the study of the function of living beings and has always tried to answer one question: what is life? Its approach is to divide function into smaller processes (mastication, digestion, absorption, metabolism, excretion...). Its history is shaped by three dualisms: on the concept of life, vitalism (peculiar life forces, linked to soul/spirit) versus mechanism (physical and chemical forces, materialism); on the method, teleology (the doctrine of purpose) versus empiricism (pure observation); on strategy, speculation (armchair physiology) versus experimentation.

QuestionOne sideOther side
What is life?Vitalism (life forces, soul)Mechanism (physics and chemistry)
How to know?Teleology (purpose)Empiricism (observation)
How to study?Speculation (armchair)Experimentation

Antiquity: life as a balance of the four elements and four humours, and the strength of three spirits — natural spirit (blood made from food in the liver), vital spirit (blood imbued with air in the lungs) and animal spirit (source of motion, in the brain). Galen: blood formed in the liver and flowing outward from the heart like irrigation water, with imaginary pores in the heart (human dissection was forbidden), and a teleological scheme of faculties for each organ (attractive, retentive, alterative, eliminative). In medieval times Galen's physiology suited the Church (life force = soul) and was repeated without expressed doubt until the 15th–16th centuries. Ibn al-Nafis described pulmonary circulation in the 13th century, unknown in Europe until translated; Michael Servetus was burned alive in 1553 after describing it.

William Harvey (17th c., English) showed blood circulates through lungs and body rather than being constantly renewed, and that the heart is a pump, by mathematics and experiment — the first serious challenge to Galen and the start of experimental physiology. Galileo: measure all that is measurable. René Descartes: mind-body dualism, explaining life by mechanical laws without denying God; animal spirits as fast particles in nerves; the soul only human, in the pineal gland; the heart heats rather than pumps; iatromechanism — the human as a clock. Critics noted passions and emotions link mind and body. Iatrochemistry: life as combustion — John Mayow's candle and mouse: breathable air and burnable air are identical, life as combustion of carbon with oxygen, heat as life. Luigi Galvani (18th c.) discovered animal electricity: current produces reflex movement.

Positivism (Auguste Comte). Dead bodies for anatomy, living animals for (often cruel) experiments. Discoveries: the respiratory centre in the medulla (Legallois), motor and sensory nerve roots (Bell-Magendie law). Magendie founded one of the first physiology journals (1821) and physiology got its own institutes and chairs. Claude Bernard (Lyon): observe a phenomenon, localise it to a structure, surgically alter it and study the effect; the organism maintains a constant milieu intérieur (homeostasis); "the great experimental principle is doubt". William Beaumont (USA) studied digestion through Alexis St. Martin's gastric fistula — an example that discovery depends on prepared insight, not just chance.

Closer physiology–medicine relationship; first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (1901); physiology entered medical education (Osler); life processes reduced to physicochemical terms; psychiatry and psychology became physiological from the 1950s; specialisation (e.g. neurosciences). Research ethics: experiments on animals and on humans (accident survivors, researchers such as Santorio and student volunteers, disadvantaged people — prisoners, soldiers, prostitutes, racial minorities); Nazi experiments on prisoners in WWII led to the Nuremberg Code (1947): voluntary informed consent, useful results for society, based on prior animal/lab work, avoid unnecessary suffering, no experiment expected to cause death or disability, risk not exceeding humanitarian importance, proper facilities, qualified researchers, right to withdraw, obligation to stop if harm appears. Then the Declaration of Helsinki (1968) and PETA (1980). Positivism still prevails, but the "why" remains seductive.

"Any fool can take off a leg. It takes a surgeon to save one" (George Ross). Medicine is science, wisdom, work of the mind; surgery is technical skill, work of the hand — from the Greek for work and hand. It is the oldest medical activity: warfare produced dangerous survival techniques, then safer compensatory techniques, then peacetime applications; urgent surgery (necessity) preceded elective surgery (intention), a complex and cautious choice.

Trephinated skulls (10,000 BC) and mandibular surgery (12,000 BC, Tafoughalt/Pigeons' cave in Morocco); splints for fractures (2400 BC); army-ant bites used as sutures. The Babylonian code punished malpractice: replace a harmed slave, but if a free man was hurt the surgeon's hands were cut off (Louvre). The Edwin Smith Papyrus (1600 BC), interpreted by James Henry Breasted in 1930, is an Egyptian surgical treatise of 48 case reports with diagnosis and management; embalming and mummification allowed experimentation with sutures. Medieval surgery was dominated by Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (Abulcasis), translated into Latin: bloodletting, cautery, operations and instruments.

Ambroise Paré (1510–1590), father of surgery: "I bandage them but God heals them". Physicians were scientists reading Greek, university-educated, meeting patients after graduation; surgeons came from the barber class, often illiterate, trained by apprenticeship and learning by doing. Professionalisation: Royal College of Physicians 1518, Royal College of Surgeons of England 1843; French surgeons rose to eminence with the Napoleonic wars. Two main challenges: pain and infection. Anaesthesia: alcohol, opium and bleeding to induce fainting; ether (1840s) brought the word "anaesthesia"; chloroform (1845); deaths on the table and post-operative complications remained. Antisepsis/asepsis: Semmelweis (1847) hand-washing with chlorinated lime; Lister (1867) carbolic acid on open fractures; rubber gloves patented (1878) — asepsis preferred over antisepsis.

The century of the surgeon: first gall-bladder operation 1867; first description of acute appendicitis 1889 (Charles McBurney); first surgeon Nobel laureate 1909 (Theodor Kocher); first open-heart operation 1952 (Walton Lillehei, hypothermia); first kidney transplant 1954 (Joseph Murray, Nobel 1990); first successful heart transplant 1967 (Christiaan Barnard, South Africa); plastic surgery developed because of wars; less invasive procedures (laparoscopy, microsurgery, laser). Polemics: cost-effectiveness of expensive procedures, and aesthetic surgery versus medical necessity.

YearFirstSurgeon
1867Gall-bladder operation—
1889Description of acute appendicitisCharles McBurney
1909Surgeon Nobel laureateTheodor Kocher
1952Open-heart operation (hypothermia)Walton Lillehei
1954Kidney transplantJoseph Murray (Nobel 1990)
1967Successful heart transplantChristiaan Barnard

"Concern for man himself and his fate must always form the chief interest of all technical endeavors" (Einstein, 1931). René Laennec (1781–1826), concerned with modesty and hygiene, could not put his ear to a lady's chest in 1816, rolled a notebook into a cylinder and was astonished to hear the heartbeat. After many prototypes he described the sounds of lungs and heart in detail; the stethoscope was the first diagnostic instrument to gain international popularity, and anatomical changes could now be detected in the living. He died of tuberculosis at 45, examined with his own invention, and warned colleagues to listen not only to patients' chests but to their stories.

Van Leeuwenhoek (Dutch, 1670) opened microscopic pathology and tissue understanding; Ramón y Cajal described synapses and initiated the neuron theory (Nobel 1906). The electron microscope (Ruska, 1931; Nobel 1986) extended vision to the molecular level and cellular functioning. Photography (1820s) was widely used in teaching pathology and in the study of movement (chronophotography). The Asilomar conference (1975) gathered 140 biologists, physicians, lawyers and science writers on the responsible use of recombinant DNA — bacteria producing human proteins, extensive use in diagnosis and therapy, stem cells and bioethics. Consequences of technology: irrefutable benefits in diagnosis and treatment; a revolution in the concept of disease (before and after the stethoscope), with high blood pressure as the example of a disease defined by an instrument; paradoxes and side effects of technological advances; and the question — what is normality?
